leading_positions.synthesis: All six members name Mircea Cărtărescu as the sole laureate in their round-1 preferred configuration, and all six also ranked him first in the opening. The shared grounds are a distinctive voice, large-scale formal patterning, and memory, the body and dream treated as one metaphysical project, with Blinding and Solenoid as the public touchstones. The case is not fully shared. The citation wordings differ on how much weight poetry carries: Palm's names only Romanian prose, Sem-Sandberg's names prose and poetry jointly, and Carlberg, Olsson, Mattson and Sward treat poetry as a root or base of the prose project. Every member records the same reservations: translation of dense Romanian prose, thinner translated coverage of the poetry and early work, and whether the longest books show depth or excess. Convergence on the ballot is not offered as evidence of merit; several members say so explicitly. Each member also gave a different set of alternatives, and none of these alternatives is a preferred configuration.

areas_of_agreement: All six preferred configurations contain a single prize part with one named writer, Mircea Cărtărescu (B026). No member proposes a multiwriter configuration or a different laureate as a first preference.

Members base the Cărtărescu case on voice, formal ambition across very large structures, and imaginative depth. Each says it should not rest on one title, on national or European representation, or on a generic period label such as 'postmodern' (stated explicitly by Mattson and Olsson).

Every member lists translation as the main limit on judgment: the density, rhythm and musicality of the Romanian prose, and thinner translated coverage of the poetry and early work than of the major novels.

Members agree that public political commentary must be kept separate from literary assessment. Olsson raised this for Adonis, Mattson extended it to every candidate including Alexis Wright, and Sward and Sem-Sandberg endorsed the principle.

Members agree that Cărtărescu's oeuvre looks consolidated enough that premature judgment is not the main concern (explicit in Olsson, Mattson, Palm, Sem-Sandberg and Sward). Palm and Olsson still treat sustained quality across the whole body of work as a question to test.

Members agree that any Carson citation would have to rest on her original written poetry, essays and verse narrative. Carlberg, Mattson, Palm and Olsson say this explicitly, and Sem-Sandberg raises the related concern about works that depend on physical design. Scholarship, translation and object-books would be context only.
No member claims to have read the corpus or independently verified any bibliography. All judgments rest on general public knowledge and colleagues' stated views.
scientific_disputes: Depth versus excess in Cărtărescu: all six name the risk that the maximalist, digressive long forms read as repetition rather than architecture. Palm adds a concrete test, asking whether the late novels deepen their image systems or only recirculate them. No member claims to have settled this.

Can Xue, rigor versus repetition: she was ranked 2nd by Mattson and Olsson, 3rd by Carlberg, 5th by Palm and Sward, and 8th by Sem-Sandberg. Mattson and Olsson read the consistent method as sustained distinctiveness, while Sem-Sandberg reads it as a question about development. Palm, Sward, Carlberg and Mattson all say partial translation prevents a firm answer.

Carson's hybrid forms: Carlberg, Palm and Sem-Sandberg rank her 2nd and Mattson ranks her 3rd. Olsson and Sward rank her 4th, citing the cumulative weight of short or fragmentary work, and Sem-Sandberg, Mattson and Palm raise the same point alongside the question of fit with the will. Palm and Sem-Sandberg add that some of the strongest books depend on physical design.

Adonis: Olsson, Palm and Sward rank him 3rd and Carlberg 4th, while Mattson and Sem-Sandberg rank him 6th. Mattson says her lower rank reflects her limits in judging Arabic prosody in translation. Sem-Sandberg says he cannot separate historical influence from the quality of the poems themselves. Nobody disputes his significance as such.

Michon: Sem-Sandberg (3rd), Mattson and Palm (4th) and Olsson (5th) accept very high sentence-level achievement. They disagree on whether a compact oeuvre and a style tied to the French sentence can support a lifetime citation. Carlberg ranks him 6th and Sward 8th.

Kind of achievement: Sward says that if the committee valued formal reinvention of a language or genre over expansion of an established visionary mode, Tawada or Adonis would have a stronger claim than Cărtărescu. Sward does not hold this as a preference, but it frames a different weighting of the common criteria.

Tawada: Sward ranks her 2nd, Carlberg and Sem-Sandberg rank her 5th, and the others did not rank her in the top eight. Several members say her wordplay and bilingual corpus cannot be judged without competence in both Japanese and German. Sem-Sandberg's impression that the later work is lighter than the best books is unconfirmed and attributed only to him.
attribution_disputes: No dispute over who the laureate should be: all six preferred configurations name Cărtărescu alone, and no organization, translator or extra name has been introduced.

Citation scope for Cărtărescu: the six wordings differ in emphasis. Carlberg names 'Romanian fiction and poetry', Sem-Sandberg 'Romanian prose and poetry', Olsson and Mattson prose with roots or grounding in poetry, Sward a Romanian-language oeuvre in prose rooted in poetry, and Palm prose only. Carlberg's response to Olsson would anchor the citation on the novels, with the poetry as origin rather than an independently assessed pillar. Mattson calls the poetry-as-base claim a hypothesis, not an established fact. Round 2 should settle one wording basis.
Citation scope for Carson, if she were considered: it would have to separate original poetic work from scholarship, translation and object-based books (Carlberg, Palm, Olsson, Sem-Sandberg).

Tawada's two-language practice: Sward, Carlberg and Mattson treat it as part of the achievement and not as an attribution problem. The open issue is evidentiary, namely which works in each language carry the case.
Adonis: members want a citation grounded in the texts, with public political positions kept out of the literary case (Olsson, Sward, Sem-Sandberg, Mattson).
maturity_disputes: Cărtărescu: no member argues the oeuvre is premature, and several cite Solenoid as a late culmination. The open question is whether sustained quality holds across the whole body of work and not only the peak novels. Palm conditions this on whether later volumes deepen or merely extend the earlier image systems. Olsson says durability across the longest works cannot be settled from reputation alone.
Poetry and early work: translated coverage is thinner, so the claim of one coherent oeuvre across genres is partly inferred (Olsson, Mattson, Palm, Carlberg, Sem-Sandberg, Sward).
Can Xue: whether four decades of a consistent method show development or restatement cannot be judged from a partial translated corpus (Mattson, Sem-Sandberg, Sward, Palm, Olsson).

Carson and Michon: members differ on whether many short or fragmentary books (Carson), or a deliberately small oeuvre (Michon), add up to significance across a body of work, in comparison with a large sustained project.
Adonis: Sward and Mattson state that his maturity is not in doubt, since the work spans roughly seven decades. The reservation is about linguistic access, not about maturity.
conflict_or_recusal_flags: No member reports a recusal-relevant connection to any shortlisted writer. Each conflict note describes only collegial, family or institutional ties and treats the member's own literary practice as context rather than evidence of preference.

Carlberg is a co-opted member, and her actual committee voting status is undocumented. Her simulated vote is a modeling assumption, and she says so in her own file. Her documented ties are to a spouse and to colleagues, not to any shortlisted writer.
Sem-Sandberg lists election alongside Carlberg and long ties to Swedish culture sections and Central European literary milieus. He names no connection to a shortlisted writer.

As chair I am also a supporter of B026 and an author of one round-1 file. My profile lists no connection to any shortlisted writer, and my scholarly interests (modern poetry, the fragment, exile literature, Celan) are context, not evidence of preference. These flags are disclosed and not adjudicated.
questions_for_round2: Can any member, citing specific volumes of the Orbitor sequence and Solenoid, show whether the long novels develop their image systems or recirculate them? What evidence in the work or in Romanian-language criticism would move members from 'excess' to 'architecture', or the reverse?

Should a Cărtărescu citation be anchored on the novels, with poetry named only as an origin (Carlberg's position), or should it name prose and poetry jointly (Sem-Sandberg's wording)? How far does the thin translated coverage of the poetry bear on that choice?

For Can Xue, what concrete evidence of variation in consciousness, form or social space across the translated corpus would distinguish rigor from repetition? Would that evidence change any member's ranking, especially Sem-Sandberg's 8th and Palm's and Sward's 5th?

Can a Carson citation be defined around original poetry, verse narrative and essays alone, with scholarship, translation and book-design excluded? If so, does the will's reference to work in an ideal direction accommodate genre-crossing work, and does the cumulative weight of her short or fragmentary books suffice?

Adonis: can members able to read Arabic, or with trusted access to it, speak to the formal quality of the poems independently of historical influence? How should the committee keep his public political positions out of the literary case?

Michon and Tawada: which specific works would carry a whole-oeuvre case, and can members judge them with confidence given the dependence on French syntax and on the Japanese and German bodies of work? Is a compact corpus a limit on significance, or only on how widely the case can be tested?

Alternatives differ across members: Carson is named by four, Can Xue and Adonis by three each, and Michon and Tawada by one each. If the Cărtărescu reservations proved weightier than currently stated, which alternative would members choose and on what grounds? Would any member regard the no-award option (P000) as preferable to the evidence now available?
summary.chair_observation: The round-1 record shows strong alignment on the single-writer configuration B026 (Mircea Cărtărescu): six of six explicit preferences, with identical laureate and citation wordings that differ mainly in how they treat poetry. The alignment rests on shared reasoning about voice, formal ambition and imaginative depth, and the shared reservations are about evidence (translation, thin coverage of the poetry, possible repetition in long forms), not about the writer's significance. That caveat matters because no member has read the corpus for this exercise, and several say a unanimous opening is not itself merit. The minority positions are stated in individual terms: Carson, Can Xue and Adonis as serious alternatives, and Sward's view that reinvention of a language or genre could outweigh scale. B039 (Alexis Wright) and B005 (Marilynne Robinson) received little explicit discussion beyond their opening ranks. This summary is a process note, not a ruling, and it reports only positions explicit in the six round-1 files.
